abstract: Manipulating visually identical objects with different physical properties requires adapting actions based on information acquired through interaction. We address the problem of learning from demonstrations how to adapt manipulation actions, such as regrasping and changing contact locations, based on physical-property information acquired during interaction. To this end, we propose a learning-from-demonstration method that learns latent representations of physical properties needed to predict object responses and conditions a policy on online estimates of these representations. A dynamics model and object-specific latent representations are jointly learned from demonstrations that include behaviors adapting to the objects’ physical properties, and the learned representations are then used to condition an imitation policy. During execution, the dynamics model and policy weights remain fixed, while the latent representation is updated based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual observations, allowing interaction with the object to inform action generation. Real-world and simulation experiments with objects whose centers of mass differ suggest that online adaptation through latent representations of physical properties can improve task success rates. However, in simulation, success rates on center-of-mass locations absent from the demonstrations remained around 30%, indicating limited adaptation to unseen physical properties. Project page: https://isri-aist.github.io/latent-dynamics-project-page/

sections.body: The section motivates learning from demonstration for visually identical objects whose centers of mass or friction differ. Corrective actions such as regrasping or changing contact locations depend on properties inferred during interaction. The proposed imitation method learns online adaptation to these properties. The stated contributions are that interaction data in manipulation demonstrations can yield implicit representations of property differences, and that combining learning from demonstration with dynamics-based property estimation improves performance on tasks with visually identical objects, including deformable objects.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Adaptive manipulation needs information gathered through interaction, which this work pairs with learning from demonstration.

sections.body: The section places the work among physical property estimation, history-dependent imitation, and world models. Earlier learning from demonstration methods obtain physical representations in a dedicated exploration phase before task execution. Recurrent and observation-window policies retain history in an internal state. The closest world-model methods update adaptation parameters or use keyframes. This method instead updates only the latent physical representation from dynamics prediction errors during execution, keeping the dynamics model and policy weights fixed.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work estimates physical properties through exploration or observation history, while this method updates only a latent representation online.

sections.body: A variational autoencoder is trained on demonstration images, and its encoder is then frozen. A learnable embedding `d_i` is shared across all timesteps and demonstrations of each object type and is initialized to 0.2i. An MLP dynamics model and these embeddings are jointly optimized to minimize prediction error. A Diffusion Policy is then trained on observations conditioned on the fixed learned embeddings. During deployment, the estimate starts from a plausible assumption and is updated by gradient descent on prediction error while the model and policy stay fixed. A retraining variant reruns the encoder and dynamics model on augmented rollout data, keeping the policy fixed.
sections.heading: Proposed Method
sections.headline: A dynamics model and a per-object latent parameter are learned from demonstrations, then only that parameter is updated during deployment.

sections.body: Pouch Placement and Box Pushing run on a real xArm7 robot, and Horizontal Lifting runs in simulation. Evaluation covers unseen center-of-mass locations in Box Pushing and Horizontal Lifting. Table I gives 12 (36) demonstrations and 3 (9) evaluation rollouts for Pouch Placement, 10 (50) demonstrations and 2 (22) evaluation rollouts for Box Pushing, and 25 (75) demonstrations and 10 (70) evaluation rollouts for Horizontal Lifting. Each method is trained with three random seeds. The dynamics model uses a prediction horizon of 14 steps, approximately 1.8 s in the real-world experiments and 1.3 s in simulation.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Experiments use two real-robot tasks and one simulation task, with objects whose centers of mass differ and held-out positions.

sections.body: On the real robot, the proposed method reached 66.7% on Pouch Placement versus 40.7% for standard Diffusion Policy. On Box Pushing, the proposed method before retraining performed similarly to the baseline. After retraining on augmented rollouts, success rose by approximately 15 percentage points. In simulation, Horizontal Lifting reached a total success rate of 58.6 ± 2.9 for the state-based model and 58.1 ± 0.8 for the image-based model, compared with 49.0 ± 0.8 for standard Diffusion Policy. On unseen objects, the proposed variants reached 30.0 ± 6.6 and 32.5 ± 2.5, compared with 21.7 ± 5.2 for the baseline.
sections.heading: Experimental Results
sections.headline: Online adaptation raised pouch placement success from 40.7% to 66.7% and reached 32.5% on unseen lifting positions.

sections.body: The section states that the method does not always estimate the physical representation reliably from brief interactions. Delayed or inaccurate estimates were linked to inappropriate insertion attempts and unnecessary contact changes on the real robot. In simulation, success on unseen center-of-mass locations remained around 30%. The experiments varied weight position in one dimension with a scalar representation. Conditions with three-dimensional center-of-mass variation, or tasks requiring behavior switches by mass, were not evaluated. The authors propose future work with pretrained visual representations and multidimensional representations.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Estimates from brief interaction are sometimes unreliable, and success on unseen centers of mass stayed around 30%.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes that the method learns latent physical representations from demonstrations and updates them online from prediction errors during execution. Conditioning the fixed Diffusion Policy on the online estimate influenced action selection and performance. Retraining the encoder and dynamics model on augmented rollout data further improved task success while the policy stayed fixed. The authors state that evaluation was limited to one-dimensional variation in mass distribution, that Pouch Placement was evaluated only on seen configurations, and that adaptation to unseen configurations was not strong in either experiment.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Latent physical representations updated online can improve imitation, but adaptation to unseen configurations stayed limited.
